Webshare is the better choice for developers, side projects and small teams: $27.50 for 10 GB against $80 at Bright Data's list price, $225 for 100 GB against a $499 minimum plan, plus free datacenter proxies for testing. Bright Data is the better choice for hardened targets and enterprise pipelines, where its pool depth, carrier and ZIP targeting worldwide, mobile network (Webshare has none) and Web Unlocker save engineering time. If you are unsure, start on Webshare and move hard targets to Bright Data later.

Bright Data and Webshare are both well-known names, but they serve opposite customers. Bright Data is the enterprise web-data platform with a 150M+ pool, carrier-level targeting and managed unblocking, SERP and browser products. Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers, with an 80M+ advertised pool, low monthly residential prices and a permanent free datacenter plan. This comparison shows when Webshare is enough and when Bright Data is worth its price.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers. It gives away 10 shared datacenter proxies with 1 GB a month forever, sells paid datacenter lists from $2.99 for 100 proxies, and offers static ISP and rotating residential networks with a clean dashboard and good API. Its rotating residential pool is listed at 80M+ IPs in 195 countries, with sticky sessions from one minute to 24 hours. The main catch is that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days and does not roll over.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
Pricing: Bright Data vs Webshare

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.

At 10 GB a month, Webshare is the cheaper option at about $27.50 against $80 for Bright Data, roughly 66% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $225 with Webshare and $499 with Bright Data: a 55% saving in Webshare's favour. Both Bright Data and Webshare work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Bright Data (150M+) is about 1.9x larger than Webshare (80M+). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and Webshare lists 195. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and Webshare offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. How Webshare compares: low prices and a developer-friendly API.
SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. The limitation on the Webshare side: fine for light rank tracking.

Social media and multi-account management: Webshare wins. The deciding factor for Webshare: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs. The limitation on the Bright Data side: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. The limitation on the Webshare side: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. The limitation on the Webshare side: no mobile network and limited selector combinations.
Tight budgets: Webshare. Webshare has the edge here. Why: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. Webshare: ID checks only when flagged or for restricted categories. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and Webshare before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Bright Data vs Webshare faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, Webshare in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
